passage.title: The Language of Bees
passage.subtitle: How one scientist discovered that honeybees can tell each other where to find food

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For centuries, beekeepers noticed that when one honeybee found a rich patch of flowers, many others from the same hive soon arrived at the same place. Some believed the bees simply followed one another, or that they found the flowers by smell alone. The real explanation was far more surprising, and it took an Austrian scientist, Karl von Frisch, several decades of careful observation to uncover it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Von Frisch began his experiments in the 1910s. He placed dishes of sugar water near his hives and marked the visiting bees with small dots of paint so that he could recognise individuals. Back inside the hive, which he had fitted with a glass wall, he watched what the marked bees did after they returned. Rather than simply unloading their food, the foragers performed a series of rapid movements on the vertical surface of the honeycomb, and other bees crowded around them, following each step closely.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Von Frisch identified two main types of movement. When the food was close to the hive, usually within about 50 metres, the returning bee ran in small circles, first in one direction and then the other. This 'round dance' told the other bees only that food was nearby; it did not indicate any particular direction. When the food was further away, the bee performed what became known as the 'waggle dance'. It ran forward in a straight line while shaking its body from side to side, then circled back to the starting point and repeated the movement.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The straight part of the waggle dance contains remarkably precise information. Its angle, measured against the vertical, shows the angle between the food source and the sun. A bee that dances straight upwards is telling the others to fly directly towards the sun, while a run pointing straight down means the food lies in the opposite direction. The length of the waggle run indicates distance: the longer the bee waggles, the further the others must fly. Because the sun moves across the sky during the day, dancing bees gradually adjust the angle of their dance, even when they have spent a long time inside the dark hive.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Not every scientist accepted these findings. In the 1960s, some researchers argued that recruited bees actually located food by following scent, and that the dance was of little practical use. The debate was not fully settled until later studies tracked individual bees with radar and showed that recruits flew almost directly to the area indicated by the dance before using smell to find the exact flowers. Von Frisch himself was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1973, sharing it with two other researchers of animal behaviour.
